data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The dominant cross-city modulator of nocturnal UHI is anthropogenic heat flux from vehicles, buildings, and industry; cities with higher nighttime energy use and population density release more sensible heat directly into the urban boundary layer, maintaining a larger temperature gap.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If nocturnal UHI is larger in low-population, low-energy cities than in high-population ones, anthropogenic heat is not the dominant modulator.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the diurnal pattern of UHI peaks before sunset rather than after, anthropogenic heat may be secondary to storage.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If reducing anthropogenic emissions does not decrease the nocturnal UHI gap in controlled studies, this mechanism is insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"On clear, calm nights, anthropogenic heat emissions add sensible heat directly to the urban atmosphere, offsetting radiative cooling. The magnitude of the nocturnal UHI scales with population density and energy consumption, because these are proxies for the rate of anthropogenic heat injection. Cities with larger populations or higher per-capita energy use thus maintain a greater night-time temperature excess over the countryside.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
